title: Log Analysis Tools: Key Features and 10 Top Picks
content_md: Most investigations stall on a simple question: where are the logs, and how do I get them out? On Windows, event logs sit in %SystemRoot%\System32\winevt\Logs\ as binary .evtx files. Export them from Event Viewer (right-click a log, then Save All Events As… ) or from an elevated prompt with wevtutil epl Security C:\IR\Security.evtx. On systemd-based Linux, the journal lives in /var/log/journal/ when persistent storage is enabled, or /run/log/journal/ when it is volatile, and journalctl -o json writes it out as one JSON object per line. Classic text syslog remains in /var/log/auth.log on Debian and Ubuntu, or /var/log/secure on RHEL-family hosts. Cloud and SaaS platforms expose their audit trails as JSON through the console or API. Getting the file is the easy part. The hard part starts when a single host hands you 400,000 events, the clock is running, and legal wants to know who sees the raw data. This is where the top AI-driven log analytics tools separate from plain search consoles. Some apply machine-learning models on top of a SIEM. Others, like SOC Prime’s LogTotal , match every event against a precompiled detection library and return correlated attack chains, not a list of hits. This guide covers what log analysis tools do, which features matter during incident response, ten tools worth knowing in 2026, and a step-by-step workflow for exporting Windows and Linux logs and investigating them in LogTotal. It closes with troubleshooting steps and answers to common questions
